name: Pacific Ocean
summary: The largest and deepest ocean, covering about a third of Earth's surface.
overview: The Pacific is the largest single feature on Earth's surface: at about 165 million km² it is bigger than all the land combined and holds roughly half of the planet's free water. It stretches about 15,500 km from the Bering Strait to Antarctica and nearly 20,000 km from Indonesia to Colombia. Its name, 'peaceful sea', came from Magellan in 1520, but it is the most geologically violent ocean, ringed by the Ring of Fire. Its tropical belt generates the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the most important source of year-to-year climate variability on the planet.
geography: Bounded by Asia and Australia to the west, the Americas to the east and the Southern Ocean to the south (about 60°S). Marginal seas include the Bering, Okhotsk, Japan, Yellow, East and South China, Philippine, Coral and Tasman seas. More than 25,000 islands lie in the Pacific, more than in all other oceans combined, grouped into Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.
water: Two great gyres (North and South Pacific) circulate clockwise and anticlockwise. The Kuroshio is the Pacific's Gulf Stream; the California and Humboldt currents carry cold water toward the equator and drive rich upwelling. The tropical Pacific warm pool is the warmest large body of ocean water. Every 2–7 years El Niño weakens the trade winds and warms the eastern Pacific, while La Niña does the opposite; the swings shift rainfall, cyclones and fisheries worldwide. The eastern tropical Pacific holds the largest oxygen minimum zone in the ocean.
life: The Coral Triangle (Indonesia, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands) holds about 76% of all known coral species and the world's richest reef fish diversity. The Great Barrier Reef is the largest living structure on Earth. Kelp forests line California and Chile. Upwelling off Peru supports the anchoveta, the largest single-species fishery. The open Pacific holds tuna, blue sharks, leatherback turtles, albatrosses and the largest whales; its trenches hold snailfish and the deepest known chemosynthetic communities.
human: About half of the world's fish catch comes from the Pacific, including tuna, pollock, anchoveta and squid. It carries the busiest container trade routes between Asia and the Americas. Pacific island nations have vast Exclusive Economic Zones that make them 'large ocean states'.
threats: Coral bleaching (the Great Barrier Reef has had repeated mass bleaching), overfishing of bluefin tuna and sharks, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, nuclear-test legacies (Bikini, Mururoa), deep-sea mining interest in the CCZ, and sea-level rise threatening atoll nations such as Tuvalu and Kiribati.
seafloor: The Pacific plate is the largest tectonic plate and is being consumed at subduction zones on almost every side. That creates the deepest trenches on Earth: Mariana (Challenger Deep, ~10,935 m), Tonga (~10,800 m), Philippine, Kuril–Kamchatka, Kermadec and Japan trenches. The East Pacific Rise spreads up to ~15 cm a year, the fastest on Earth, and hosts black-smoker vents. Tens of thousands of seamounts and guyots dot the basin, including the Hawaiian–Emperor chain that records the plate's motion over a hotspot. The Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico holds the world's richest polymetallic nodule fields.
climate_weather: The western North Pacific produces more tropical cyclones (typhoons) than any other basin, about a third of the global total, including the strongest storms on record. El Niño years bring floods to Peru, drought to Australia and Indonesia, and weaker Indian monsoons. The Pacific Decadal Oscillation shifts sea temperatures over decades, and the 2014–16 'Blob' marine heatwave killed seabirds, whales and kelp along North America.
ecosystems: Coral reefs and atolls, kelp forests, mangroves of Southeast Asia, upwelling systems (California, Humboldt), hydrothermal vents (East Pacific Rise, back-arc basins), hadal trenches, seamounts, abyssal nodule plains, and the oligotrophic central gyres that are the ocean's 'deserts'.
history: Polynesian navigators settled the Pacific's islands over thousands of years using stars, swells and birds, reaching Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand. Magellan crossed in 1520–21; Cook mapped much of it in the 1770s. HMS Challenger sounded the Mariana area in 1875, Trieste reached Challenger Deep in 1960, and Alvin found the first hydrothermal vents on the Galápagos Rift in 1977. The Pacific was the main theatre of naval warfare in World War II, leaving thousands of wrecks, from Pearl Harbor to Truk Lagoon.

name: Atlantic Ocean
summary: The second-largest ocean, split down the middle by the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and home to the AMOC.
overview: The Atlantic is the second-largest ocean (about 106 million km²) and the youngest of the major basins, opening as Pangaea broke apart around 180 million years ago. It is still widening by about 2.5 cm a year along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. It is the saltiest open ocean and the engine room of the global overturning circulation: cold, salty water sinks in the north and spreads through the deep ocean worldwide. That makes the Atlantic central to Earth's climate.
geography: An S-shaped basin between the Americas to the west and Europe and Africa to the east, from the Arctic to the Southern Ocean. Marginal seas include the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Mediterranean, North, Baltic, Norwegian and Labrador seas, plus the Sargasso Sea, the only sea with no coastline. It drains more river water than any other ocean, including the Amazon, Congo, Mississippi and Niger.
water: The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Current carry tropical heat to Europe. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) sinks water in the Labrador and Nordic seas, forming North Atlantic Deep Water. In the south, the Benguela upwelling off Namibia is one of the most productive systems on Earth. Salinity reaches ~37 PSU in the subtropics because evaporation exceeds rainfall.
life: Cold-water coral reefs off Norway and Ireland, the cod and herring stocks of the Grand Banks and North Sea, North Atlantic right whales, humpbacks breeding in the Caribbean, Atlantic bluefin tuna crossing the basin, the Sargasso Sea's floating sargassum community where European and American eels spawn, sea turtles, gannets, puffins, and the Lost City vent fauna.
human: Historic cod, herring, tuna and whale fisheries; North Sea oil and offshore wind; the busiest transatlantic shipping and cable routes.
threats: Collapse of the Grand Banks cod (1992), AMOC weakening, sargassum blooms swamping Caribbean beaches since 2011, ship strikes and entanglement of right whales, plastic accumulation in the North Atlantic gyre, and warming that pushes fish north.
seafloor: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs ~16,000 km down the centre and rises above sea level in Iceland and the Azores. Vent fields such as TAG, Rainbow and the alkaline Lost City lie along it. The deepest point is the Milwaukee Deep in the Puerto Rico Trench (~8,376 m); the South Sandwich Trench lies in the far south. Wide continental shelves (Grand Banks, North Sea, Patagonian shelf) host rich fisheries, and submarine canyons cut the margins.
climate_weather: The tropical Atlantic produces hurricanes from June to November, born from African easterly waves over warm water above ~26.5°C. The North Atlantic Oscillation steers European winters. A weakening AMOC is one of the major climate tipping-point concerns (see AMOC weakening).
ecosystems: Sargassum mats, coral reefs (Caribbean), cold-water coral mounds, seagrass and mangroves, upwelling systems (Benguela, Canary), vent and seep communities, and the abyssal plains of the Cape Verde and Sohm basins.
history: Vikings reached North America around 1000 CE; Columbus crossed in 1492. The Atlantic slave trade forcibly carried over 12 million Africans across it. Matthew Maury charted its winds and currents in the 1850s; the first transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in 1858. Famous wrecks include the Titanic (found in 1985 at ~3,800 m), Lusitania and Bismarck. Endurance, lost in the Weddell Sea in 1915, was found in 2022.

name: Indian Ocean
summary: The warmest ocean, ruled by monsoon reversals of winds and currents.
overview: The Indian Ocean (~70.5 million km²) is the third-largest and the warmest ocean. Unlike the Pacific and Atlantic, it is closed to the north by Asia, so it has no northern polar water. Instead its circulation is ruled by the monsoon: winds and major currents reverse direction twice a year. It is named after India, whose rainfall, agriculture and economy depend directly on its behaviour.
geography: Bounded by Africa to the west, Asia to the north, Australia and Indonesia to the east and the Southern Ocean to the south. Marginal seas include the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, Andaman Sea, Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Laccadive Sea and Mozambique Channel. Island groups include Madagascar, Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Lakshadweep, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Seychelles, Mauritius and Réunion. Major rivers include the Ganges–Brahmaputra, Indus, Zambezi and Irrawaddy.
water: During the southwest monsoon (June–September) the Somali Current flows north at up to ~3.5 m/s and drives strong upwelling off Somalia, Oman and western India; in the northeast monsoon it reverses. The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), a see-saw of temperatures between west and east, shapes rainfall in India, East Africa and Australia. The Agulhas Current, one of the strongest western boundary currents, leaks warm salty water into the Atlantic. The Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal hold intense oxygen minimum zones.
life: Coelacanths off South Africa and Comoros, whale sharks of the Maldives and Ningaloo, dugongs, olive ridley turtles mass-nesting in Odisha, the Sundarbans mangroves with their tigers and Ganges river dolphins, manta rays of the Maldives, hilsa migrating up the Bengal rivers, and vent fauna like the scaly-foot snail.
human: Fisheries feed hundreds of millions of people. It carries major oil routes through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb, and about 80% of global seaborne oil trade passes through it. India's Deep Ocean Mission and Samudrayaan target its depths.
threats: Fastest warming of any ocean, repeated coral bleaching (the Maldives and Lakshadweep), expanding oxygen minimum zones in the Arabian Sea, sea-level rise threatening the Maldives, plastics carried by rivers, and overfishing.
seafloor: The Java (Sunda) Trench (~7,290 m) is its deepest point and the source of the 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake and tsunami. Three ridges (Central, Southwest and Southeast Indian ridges) meet at the Rodrigues Triple Junction, where the Kairei vent field hosts the scaly-foot snail. The Bengal Fan, built by sediment from the Himalaya via the Ganges–Brahmaputra, is the largest submarine fan on Earth. The Central Indian Ocean Basin holds nodule fields explored by India under an ISA contract.
climate_weather: The Bay of Bengal produces some of the deadliest tropical cyclones in history, because a shallow, funnel-shaped bay amplifies storm surges onto the low Ganges delta. Arabian Sea cyclones have become more frequent and intense as it warms. Monsoon rain from the ocean supplies most of India's annual rainfall. The Indian Ocean is warming faster than any other ocean, intensifying marine heatwaves.
ecosystems: Coral atolls (Maldives, Lakshadweep, Chagos), the Sundarbans (the world's largest mangrove forest), seagrass meadows grazed by dugongs, upwelling systems, deep oxygen minimum zones and hydrothermal vents.
history: Monsoon winds powered trade between Africa, Arabia, India and China for over 2,000 years. Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498. The 2004 tsunami killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries and led to the Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System.

name: Southern Ocean
summary: The ring of ocean around Antarctica, driven by the strongest current on Earth.
overview: The Southern Ocean encircles Antarctica south of about 60°S and was formally recognised as the fifth ocean by the International Hydrographic Organization in 2000 (and by National Geographic in 2021). It is defined less by coastlines than by a current: the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the largest current on Earth. It is the ocean's main gateway between surface and deep water, absorbing a large share of the heat and carbon dioxide that humans add to the climate system.
geography: Surrounds Antarctica, with the Weddell, Ross, Amundsen, Bellingshausen and Scotia seas as major embayments. The Drake Passage between South America and the Antarctic Peninsula is its narrowest point. Sub-Antarctic islands such as South Georgia, Kerguelen, Heard and Macquarie are wildlife strongholds.
water: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows eastward around the continent, carrying over 100 times the flow of all the world's rivers. Antarctic Bottom Water, the densest water in the ocean, forms on the Weddell and Ross shelves as sea ice forms and rejects salt, then spreads along the floor of all oceans. Upwelling of old deep water around Antarctica brings nutrients and CO₂ back to the surface.
life: Antarctic krill (perhaps the largest biomass of any wild animal species), emperor, Adélie, chinstrap, gentoo and king penguins, Weddell, leopard and crabeater seals, blue, humpback, fin and minke whales, albatrosses and petrels, and icefish with no red blood cells. Benthic communities include giant sea spiders and slow-growing sponges.
human: Krill and toothfish fisheries regulated by CCAMLR; tourism to the Antarctic Peninsula; research stations from about 30 nations, including India's Maitri and Bharati.
threats: Warming and sea-ice loss, ocean acidification (cold water absorbs CO₂ fastest), krill fishing near penguin colonies, ice-shelf collapse and invasive species arriving on ships.
seafloor: The South Sandwich Trench (~7,400 m, the Factorian Deep) is the deepest point. Continental shelves around Antarctica are unusually deep (~500 m) because the weight of the ice sheet pushes the crust down. Mid-ocean ridges and seamounts steer the circumpolar current.
climate_weather: Westerly winds are the strongest on Earth ('Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Screaming Sixties'). Sea ice expands each winter to about 18 million km² and shrinks to ~3 million km² in summer; record lows since 2016, and especially 2023, have alarmed scientists. Warm water reaching beneath ice shelves (Thwaites, Pine Island) threatens future sea-level rise.
ecosystems: Sea-ice ecosystems (algae under ice), krill-based food webs, sub-Antarctic island seabird and seal colonies, deep continental shelves, and the ice-shelf cavities beneath floating ice.
history: Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle in 1773. Sealers and whalers devastated fur seals and great whales in the 19th and 20th centuries. The Antarctic Treaty (1959) set the continent aside for peace and science; CCAMLR (1982) manages its marine life. Shackleton's Endurance sank in the Weddell Sea in 1915 and was found at 3,008 m in 2022.

name: Arctic Ocean
summary: The smallest, shallowest ocean, losing its summer sea ice fast.
overview: The Arctic is the smallest (~15.6 million km²) and shallowest ocean, mostly enclosed by Eurasia and North America. Much of it is covered by sea ice that grows and shrinks with the seasons. It is warming about four times faster than the global average, so its ice cover is one of the clearest signals of climate change.
geography: Ringed by Russia, Norway, Greenland, Canada and Alaska. Marginal seas include the Barents, Kara, Laptev, East Siberian, Chukchi and Beaufort seas, plus Baffin Bay and Hudson Bay. The Fram Strait is the main deep connection to the Atlantic; the narrow Bering Strait links it to the Pacific.
water: The Beaufort Gyre stores fresh water from rivers and melting ice, and the Transpolar Drift carries ice from Siberia toward Fram Strait. Huge Siberian rivers (Ob, Yenisei, Lena) make the surface fresher than any other ocean. Atlantic water entering through the Barents Sea is warming the Arctic from below ('Atlantification').
life: Polar bears, walruses, ringed and bearded seals, narwhals, belugas and bowhead whales, polar cod living in ice cracks, ice algae, Arctic char, little auks and ivory gulls. The Bering and Barents seas host some of the richest fisheries on Earth.
human: Indigenous subsistence hunting, Barents Sea and Bering Sea fisheries, Arctic shipping routes opening as ice melts (the Northern Sea Route), and oil and gas exploration.
threats: Rapid ice loss, Atlantification, shipping and oil-spill risk, microplastics trapped in sea ice, and fisheries moving north into unregulated waters (a central Arctic fishing moratorium was agreed in 2018).
seafloor: The Arctic has the widest continental shelves on Earth, especially off Siberia, holding about half its area. The Lomonosov Ridge divides it into the Amerasian and Eurasian basins; the Gakkel Ridge is the slowest-spreading ridge on Earth yet hosts active vents (the Aurora field). The deepest point is the Molloy Deep (~5,550 m) in the Fram Strait.
climate_weather: September sea-ice extent has fallen by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979, and multi-year ice has largely disappeared. Loss of white ice exposes dark water that absorbs more sunlight, accelerating warming (ice–albedo feedback). Thawing subsea permafrost may release methane.
ecosystems: Sea-ice ecosystems, polynyas (open-water oases in ice), shallow Siberian shelves, the Barents Sea cod system and vents on the Gakkel Ridge.
history: Inuit and other Indigenous peoples have lived along its coasts for millennia. Searches for the Northwest Passage killed Franklin's 1845 expedition; its ships Erebus and Terror were found in 2014 and 2016. Nansen's Fram drifted across it in 1893–96; the submarine USS Nautilus passed under the North Pole in 1958.

name: Mediterranean Sea
summary: A nearly enclosed sea with unusually warm, salty deep water and a long human history.
overview: A nearly enclosed sea of about 2.5 million km² linking Europe, Africa and Asia, connected to the Atlantic only by the 14 km-wide Strait of Gibraltar. It is a remnant of the ancient Tethys Ocean and has been the stage for Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Arab, Venetian and Ottoman sea power for 4,000 years. Because evaporation exceeds river input, it is saltier and warmer than the Atlantic.
geography: It stretches about 3,800 km from Gibraltar to the Levant and is divided by Sicily and Tunisia into western and eastern basins, with sub-seas including the Alboran, Balearic, Ligurian, Tyrrhenian, Adriatic, Ionian, Aegean and Levantine seas. It connects to the Black Sea through the Dardanelles and Bosporus and to the Red Sea through the Suez Canal (1869).
water: Atlantic surface water flows in at Gibraltar while dense, salty Mediterranean water (about 38–39 PSU) sinks and flows out beneath it, spreading through the Atlantic at around 1,000 m depth. Surface waters have warmed by more than 1 °C since the 1980s, and marine heatwaves pushed summer temperatures near 30 °C in 2022–2024.
life: Despite covering under 1% of the ocean, it holds roughly 7–10% of known marine species, including the Mediterranean monk seal, loggerhead and green turtles, fin and sperm whales, bluefin tuna, and the endemic seagrass Posidonia oceanica, whose meadows can be thousands of years old.
human: About 150 million people live on its coasts and over 300 million tourists visit each year. Fisheries, shipping (around a fifth of world shipping passes through) and offshore gas in the Levant basin are major industries.
threats: It is one of the most overfished seas, with most assessed stocks fished beyond sustainable levels, and a hotspot for plastic pollution and warming. Migrant crossings make the central Mediterranean the deadliest migration route in the world.
seafloor: The seafloor is tectonically active where the African plate pushes under Europe, creating the volcanoes of Etna, Vesuvius, Stromboli and Santorini and the deep Hellenic Trench, whose Calypso Deep (~5,267 m) is the sea's deepest point. About 5.96–5.33 million years ago the Strait of Gibraltar closed and the sea nearly dried out (the Messinian salinity crisis), leaving salt layers over a kilometre thick; it refilled in the Zanclean flood.
climate_weather: A hot, dry-summer 'Mediterranean climate'. It is warming ~20% faster than the global ocean, with repeated marine heatwaves since 2003 causing mass die-offs of gorgonians and the noble pen shell. 'Medicanes' (Mediterranean hurricane-like storms) such as Daniel in 2023 caused catastrophic floods in Libya.
ecosystems: Posidonia seagrass meadows, coralligenous reefs of encrusting red algae, deep cold-water coral mounds, and lagoons such as the Venice lagoon. More than 1,000 non-native species, many arriving through the Suez Canal ('Lessepsian migrants') such as lionfish and rabbitfish, are reshaping the eastern basin.
history: The cradle of Western seafaring: Minoan, Phoenician, Greek and Roman fleets; the Antikythera mechanism shipwreck; the battles of Salamis, Actium and Lepanto; Venetian and Genoese trade empires. Shipwrecks litter its floor from the Bronze Age Uluburun wreck onward.

name: Caribbean Sea
summary: A tropical sea of coral reefs and the deepest point of the Caribbean, the Cayman Trough.
overview: A tropical sea of about 2.75 million km² bounded by the Antilles island arcs, Central America and northern South America. It is famous for coral reefs, clear blue water and hurricanes, and for being the first region of the Americas reached by Columbus in 1492.
geography: It lies on the Caribbean plate, framed by the Greater Antilles (Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica, Puerto Rico) to the north and the Lesser Antilles volcanic arc to the east. It connects to the Gulf of Mexico through the Yucatán Channel and to the Pacific via the Panama Canal.
water: Warm (26–29 °C), clear and low in nutrients. The Caribbean Current carries water westward into the Gulf of Mexico, where it becomes the Loop Current and feeds the Gulf Stream.
life: Home to the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef (the second-largest barrier reef), staghorn and elkhorn corals, parrotfish, groupers, manatees, hawksbill and green turtles, and the vast seasonal mats of drifting Sargassum seaweed.
human: Tourism is the main industry for many island nations, alongside fishing and shipping through the Panama Canal.
threats: Coral bleaching (mass events in 2005, 2010, 2023), stony coral tissue loss disease, invasive lionfish, overfishing, Sargassum influxes and stronger hurricanes.
seafloor: Its deepest point is the Cayman Trough (~7,686 m), where an ultra-slow spreading centre hosts the world's deepest known hydrothermal vents (Beebe vent field, ~5,000 m). The Puerto Rico Trench just to the north is the deepest point of the Atlantic.
climate_weather: The core of the Atlantic hurricane belt: warm water (>26.5°C) fuels storms from June to November. Sargassum influxes since 2011 smother beaches. Repeated heatwaves have bleached most reefs.
ecosystems: Fringing and barrier reefs, mangrove forests, seagrass beds, blue holes (such as Belize's Great Blue Hole) and deep-sea vents. Many reefs have lost over half their coral cover since the 1970s.
history: Indigenous Taíno and Kalinago peoples lived on the islands before European conquest. The sea became the centre of the plantation economy and the transatlantic slave trade, and the age of pirates; wrecks of Spanish treasure galleons still lie on its floor.

name: Gulf of Mexico
summary: A basin of natural oil seeps, brine pools and a large seasonal 'dead zone'.
overview: An ocean basin of about 1.6 million km² enclosed by the USA, Mexico and Cuba. It is one of the world's main oil and gas regions and a major fishery, and the birthplace of many Atlantic hurricanes' most intense phases.
geography: Bounded by the US Gulf Coast, Mexico's coast and the Yucatán Peninsula, and connected to the Atlantic through the Florida Straits and to the Caribbean through the Yucatán Channel.
water: The Loop Current carries warm Caribbean water through the Gulf before exiting as the Florida Current, the start of the Gulf Stream. The Mississippi River pours in nutrient-rich freshwater.
life: Bottlenose dolphins, sperm whales, whale sharks, Kemp's ridley turtles (the most endangered sea turtle, nesting in Tamaulipas), red snapper, shrimp, oysters and Rice's whale, a critically endangered species described in 2021.
human: Produces about 15% of US crude oil and supports large shrimp, oyster and menhaden fisheries.
threats: A seasonal 'dead zone' of low oxygen (often 10,000–20,000 km²) forms off Louisiana from Mississippi fertiliser runoff. The 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout spilled about 4.9 million barrels of oil. Coastal Louisiana loses wetlands to subsidence and sea-level rise.
seafloor: Broad continental shelves surround a central abyssal plain reaching about 4,384 m in the Sigsbee Deep. Thick salt layers deposited ~160 million years ago form domes and trap oil. The Chicxulub crater, left by the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, lies partly beneath its southern margin.
climate_weather: The Loop Current feeds warm water that intensifies hurricanes (Katrina 2005, Harvey 2017, Ian 2022). Mississippi River nutrients create a summer 'dead zone' of hypoxic water averaging ~14,000 km².
ecosystems: Seagrass, oyster reefs, the Flower Garden Banks coral reefs, cold seeps with tubeworms and ice worms, and Kemp's ridley turtle nesting beaches.
history: Spanish explorers mapped it in the 16th century; it became the gateway for cotton and sugar exports via New Orleans. Hundreds of shipwrecks, including WWII U-boat victims, lie on its floor.

name: Sargasso Sea
summary: The only sea without coastlines, defined by currents and floating Sargassum seaweed.
overview: The only sea without a coastline, defined by ocean currents rather than land. It lies in the North Atlantic subtropical gyre and is named after Sargassum, the golden-brown seaweed that floats in vast mats on its surface.
geography: Bounded by the Gulf Stream to the west, the North Atlantic Current to the north, the Canary Current to the east and the North Atlantic Equatorial Current to the south. Bermuda lies on its western edge.
water: Exceptionally clear, deep-blue, warm and nutrient-poor, with very little plankton. Being at the centre of a gyre, it gathers floating debris, part of the North Atlantic garbage patch.
life: Sargassum mats shelter a unique community: the Sargassum fish, Sargassum shrimp and crabs, juvenile sea turtles and baby fish. European and American eels migrate thousands of kilometres to spawn here, a mystery first solved by Johannes Schmidt in the 1920s.
human: Little direct use; it is a key area for long-term ocean monitoring at the Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study (BATS), running since 1988.
threats: Plastic accumulation, shipping, and loss of eels whose numbers have collapsed by over 90% in some rivers. The Hamilton Declaration (2014) set up an international commission to protect it.
seafloor: Overlies deep abyssal plains (Nares and Hatteras) and the Bermuda Rise; about 4,500–6,500 m deep.
climate_weather: Bounded only by currents of the North Atlantic Gyre, so it has calm, clear, nutrient-poor warm water. The Bermuda Atlantic Time-series Study (since 1988) records ocean warming and acidification here.
ecosystems: Floating sargassum mats host endemic sargassum fish, crabs and nudibranchs, and nurseries for sea turtles. It is the spawning ground of European and American eels.
history: Named by Portuguese sailors; Columbus feared his ships would be trapped in its weed. The 2014 Hamilton Declaration created a commission for its conservation.

name: North Sea
summary: A shallow, heavily used shelf sea between Britain and mainland Europe.
overview: A shallow shelf sea of about 575,000 km² between Britain, Scandinavia, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France. It is one of the busiest seas on Earth for shipping, fishing, oil, gas and wind power.
geography: Connected to the Atlantic in the north and through the English Channel in the south, and to the Baltic through the Skagerrak and Kattegat.
water: Cool, well mixed by strong tides and storms, with lower salinity near river mouths such as the Rhine and Elbe.
life: Atlantic cod, herring, mackerel, plaice, harbour porpoises, grey and harbour seals, and huge seabird colonies such as gannets at Bass Rock.
human: North Sea oil and gas since the 1960s; today it is the world's leading offshore-wind region. Ports include Rotterdam, Europe's largest.
threats: Past overfishing collapsed cod stocks; pollution, seabed trawling and the industrialisation of the sea with wind farms and cables.
seafloor: A shallow shelf sea (average ~95 m) that was dry land, Doggerland, until about 8,000 years ago; fishermen still trawl up mammoth bones and Stone Age tools. The Norwegian Trench reaches ~700 m.
climate_weather: Severe winter storms and storm surges (the 1953 flood killed over 2,000 people in the Netherlands and UK). Warming has shifted cod north and brought in warm-water species.
ecosystems: The Wadden Sea, a UNESCO site of tidal flats from the Netherlands to Denmark, is one of the largest intertidal systems in the world; sandbanks such as Dogger Bank.
history: Viking routes, the Hanseatic League, the Battle of Jutland (1916) whose wrecks lie on the floor, North Sea oil since 1970 and now the world's largest offshore wind farms.

name: Baltic Sea
summary: A young brackish sea with some of the largest dead zones on Earth.
overview: A young, shallow, brackish sea of about 377,000 km² enclosed by nine countries. It is one of the largest bodies of brackish water in the world, with a mix of marine and freshwater species.
geography: Bordered by Sweden, Finland, Russia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Germany and Denmark; it includes the Gulfs of Bothnia, Finland and Riga and connects to the North Sea through the Danish straits.
water: Salinity falls from about 20 PSU near Denmark to almost fresh in the northern Gulf of Bothnia. A permanent salinity layer limits mixing, so deep water depends on rare inflows of salty North Sea water.
life: Baltic herring, cod, sprat, ringed and grey seals, harbour porpoises (the Baltic Proper population is critically endangered), and bladderwrack forests.
human: Shipping, ferries, fishing and gas pipelines; the Nord Stream pipelines were sabotaged in 2022.
threats: Has some of the world's largest dead zones (up to ~70,000 km²) from fertiliser runoff; dumped WWII chemical munitions; cod stocks collapsed and fishing for eastern Baltic cod was closed in 2019.
seafloor: Average depth only about 55 m, with a deepest point of 459 m (Landsort Deep). It formed as ice sheets melted after the last Ice Age, and parts of Scandinavia are still rising from post-glacial rebound.
climate_weather: Very low salinity (from ~2 PSU in the north to ~20 at the entrance) and limited exchange with the North Sea make it vulnerable. Its deep basins have one of the world's largest dead zones, caused by nutrient runoff.
ecosystems: A mix of marine and freshwater species, bladderwrack, grey and ringed seals, harbour porpoises, cod and herring.
history: The Hanseatic trading league, Swedish and Russian empires, and the 1628 Vasa warship, raised almost intact because the brackish water lacks shipworms. Countless wrecks are preserved.

name: Black Sea
summary: The largest anoxic body of water on Earth: below ~150–200 m there is no oxygen.
overview: An inland sea of about 436,000 km² between Europe and Asia. Below about 150–200 m its water contains no oxygen and is full of hydrogen sulphide, making it the world's largest anoxic water body.
geography: Bordered by Ukraine, Russia, Georgia, Turkey, Bulgaria and Romania; connected to the Mediterranean through the Bosporus and Dardanelles, and to the Sea of Azov. The Danube, Dnieper and Don pour in fresh water.
water: A low-salinity surface layer (about 18 PSU) sits on dense saltier water; this layering prevents oxygen from reaching the depths, so about 90% of its volume is anoxic.
life: Black Sea bottlenose dolphins, harbour porpoises, anchovy (hamsi), turbot, sturgeons (critically endangered) and the invasive comb jelly Mnemiopsis that crashed fisheries in the 1980s.
human: Fishing, ports such as Odesa and Constanța, grain exports and tourism.
threats: Pollution, invasive species, overfishing and the effects of war, including dam destruction (Kakhovka, 2023) and mines.
seafloor: A deep basin (~2,212 m) linked to the Mediterranean only by the narrow Bosporus. Below ~150 m the water has no oxygen and is full of hydrogen sulfide, the largest anoxic water body on Earth.
climate_weather: Strong stratification: a fresher surface layer from rivers (Danube, Dnieper, Don) sits above dense salty water that never mixes.
ecosystems: Surface life includes dolphins, anchovy and turbot; the sulfidic depths hold only microbes. The invasive comb jelly Mnemiopsis collapsed fisheries in the 1980s.
history: Greek colonies, the Byzantine and Ottoman empires and Crimean wars. In 2018 researchers found a 2,400-year-old Greek merchant ship, the oldest intact shipwreck known, perfectly preserved without oxygen.

name: Red Sea
summary: A young ocean in the making, with heat-tolerant corals and hot brine pools.
overview: A narrow, very salty sea of about 438,000 km² between Africa and Arabia, formed as the two continents split apart. It is famous for some of the world's most heat-tolerant coral reefs.
geography: Runs about 2,250 km from the Gulf of Suez and Gulf of Aqaba to the Bab-el-Mandeb strait and the Gulf of Aden; bordered by Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Jordan and Israel.
water: One of the saltiest seas (about 40 PSU) because of intense evaporation and no rivers, and very warm (surface often 26–32 °C).
life: Over 1,200 fish species (about 10% found nowhere else), dugongs, spinner dolphins, sharks and around 300 species of hard coral.
human: About 12% of global trade passed through it before 2024; attacks on shipping by Houthi forces from late 2023 diverted many ships around Africa.
threats: Coastal development, tourism, shipping accidents, and the decaying FSO Safer oil tanker, whose oil was transferred in 2023 to avert a disaster.
seafloor: A young ocean in the making: a spreading rift down its centre reaches about 3,040 m, with hot, salty brine pools on the seafloor that are toxic to most life.
climate_weather: Among the warmest and saltiest seas (~40 PSU) because of extreme evaporation and almost no rivers. Its northern corals are unusually heat-tolerant and may be a refuge as oceans warm.
ecosystems: Northern Red Sea corals in the Gulf of Aqaba tolerate heat that bleaches corals elsewhere, possibly making them a refuge for reefs under warming.
history: Ancient Egyptian expeditions to Punt, Roman trade with India, and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869.

name: Arabian Sea
summary: Home to one of the world's thickest oxygen minimum zones, driven by monsoon upwelling.
overview: The northwestern part of the Indian Ocean, about 3.86 million km², between India, Pakistan, Iran, Oman and the Horn of Africa. It is one of the most biologically productive seas, driven by monsoon upwelling.
geography: Includes the Gulf of Aden, Gulf of Oman and Laccadive Sea, with the Lakshadweep and Maldive islands to the southeast. Major ports include Mumbai, Karachi, Kochi and Muscat.
water: In summer the southwest monsoon drives strong upwelling off Oman and Somalia, bringing up nutrients. Below the surface lies one of the world's largest oxygen minimum zones.
life: Blue whales (a resident, non-migratory population), dolphins, sardines and mackerel that support Kerala's fisheries, whale sharks off Gujarat, and the Arabian humpback whale, the most isolated humpback population.
human: Fisheries, oil tankers from the Persian Gulf, and the ports of Mumbai and Karachi.
threats: Expanding oxygen-poor zones, warming, cyclones, overfishing and plastic.
seafloor: Deepest about 4,652 m; the Carlsberg Ridge spreads apart in the southwest, and the Indus Fan, one of the largest sediment fans in the world, spreads from the Indus delta.
climate_weather: The southwest monsoon drives intense upwelling and plankton blooms. It holds one of the world's thickest oxygen minimum zones, and cyclones have become more frequent as it warms (e.g. Tauktae 2021 and Biparjoy 2023).
ecosystems: Upwelling-driven fisheries (oil sardine, mackerel), Lakshadweep atolls and the Gulf of Kutch coral reefs.
history: Monsoon sailing linked India, Arabia, Persia and East Africa for over 2,000 years; ports like Muziris, Calicut and Surat drew traders from Rome to Portugal.

name: Bay of Bengal
summary: The world's largest bay, freshened by the Ganges–Brahmaputra and fuelling strong cyclones.
overview: The largest bay in the world, about 2.17 million km², bordered by India, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Sri Lanka. Fed by the Ganges, Brahmaputra and other great rivers, it is one of the world's most cyclone-prone and densely populated coasts.
geography: Its coasts include Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands mark its eastern edge.
water: Enormous river discharge makes its surface water relatively fresh and layered, keeping the surface warm and helping fuel cyclones.
life: Olive ridley turtles nesting in mass arribadas at Gahirmatha and Rushikulya, Irrawaddy dolphins, Bryde's whales, hilsa fish and the Sundarbans tiger.
human: Supports millions of fishers, ports and ship-breaking at Chittagong.
threats: Sea-level rise and storm surges, an expanding oxygen-poor zone, plastic and overfishing.
seafloor: Covered by the Bengal Fan, the largest submarine fan on Earth, built from Himalayan sediment and up to 16 km thick in places. The Swatch of No Ground canyon cuts into the shelf.
climate_weather: Has produced many of history's deadliest cyclones, including the 1970 Bhola cyclone (around 300,000–500,000 deaths), the 1999 Odisha super cyclone, Amphan (2020) and Fani (2019). Better warnings have cut death tolls dramatically.
ecosystems: The Sundarbans mangroves, olive ridley mass-nesting in Odisha, hilsa runs, Irrawaddy dolphins and the Andaman reefs.
history: The Chola navy, Kalinga traders to Southeast Asia, and colonial ports of Calcutta, Madras and Chittagong.

name: Coral Sea
summary: Home to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth.
overview: A tropical sea of about 4.8 million km² off northeastern Australia, home to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system on Earth.
geography: Bounded by Queensland, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia.
water: Warm and clear, driven by the East Australian Current.
life: About 1,500 fish species on the Great Barrier Reef, dugongs, green and loggerhead turtles, humpback and dwarf minke whales, and over 400 hard coral species.
human: Reef tourism and fisheries worth billions to Australia.
threats: Mass coral bleaching (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024), crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks, farm runoff and cyclones.
seafloor: Includes the Queensland Plateau and deep basins over 9,000 m in the New Hebrides Trench region; many reefs sit on submerged plateaus.
climate_weather: Cyclone-prone in the austral summer; repeated mass bleaching since 1998 (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024).
ecosystems: The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest reef system, with ~1,500 fish species, dugongs, nesting turtles and Osprey Reef sharks.
history: Site of the 1942 Battle of the Coral Sea, the first naval battle fought entirely by aircraft carriers, which halted Japan's advance toward Australia.

name: South China Sea
summary: A biodiverse and contested sea crossed by a large share of global shipping.
overview: A marginal sea of about 3.5 million km² in the western Pacific, rich in reefs, fisheries and possible oil and gas. It carries roughly a third of global maritime trade and is the scene of overlapping territorial claims.
geography: Bordered by China, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei, Indonesia and Vietnam, and containing the Spratly and Paracel islands and Scarborough Shoal.
water: Monsoon winds reverse surface currents seasonally; the Kuroshio intrudes through the Luzon Strait.
life: About a third of the world's marine biodiversity by some estimates, giant clams, dugongs, green turtles and many reef fish.
human: Fisheries employing millions and shipping through the Strait of Malacca.
threats: Island-building that destroyed reefs, giant-clam poaching, overfishing and maritime confrontations.
seafloor: Its central basin reaches about 5,016 m; it opened by seafloor spreading between ~32 and 16 million years ago.
climate_weather: Typhoon-prone; driven by the East Asian monsoon.
ecosystems: Coral reefs at the edge of the Coral Triangle, seagrass, and some of the world's most heavily fished waters.
history: Maritime Silk Road trade; today about a third of global shipping passes through, and overlapping territorial claims make it a geopolitical flashpoint.

name: Sea of Japan (East Sea)
summary: A semi-enclosed sea that forms its own deep water, like a mini-ocean.
overview: A marginal sea of about 978,000 km² between Japan, Korea and Russia, called the East Sea in Korea. It is almost enclosed, connected to other seas by shallow straits.
geography: Bounded by Honshu and Hokkaido, the Korean Peninsula and the Russian Far East, with the Tsushima, Tsugaru, La Pérouse and Tatar straits.
water: Has its own cold, oxygen-rich deep water formed in winter off Vladivostok; the warm Tsushima Current flows in from the south.
life: Snow crabs, squid, Pacific saury, salmon, spotted seals and Steller sea lions.
human: Fisheries and shipping between Japan, Korea, China and Russia.
threats: Warming faster than the global average, declining deep-water oxygen and overfishing.
seafloor: Deep basins reach about 3,742 m; the sea opened as Japan split from the Asian mainland ~20–15 million years ago.
climate_weather: Cold winter monsoon winds form deep water locally; this formation has weakened with warming.
ecosystems: Snow crabs, firefly squid (Toyama Bay), Japanese flying squid and Pacific saury.
history: The 1905 Battle of Tsushima. The sea's name is disputed (Korea uses 'East Sea').

name: Bering Sea
summary: One of the most productive seas on Earth, supporting huge pollock and crab fisheries.
overview: A cold, highly productive sea of about 2 million km² between Alaska and Russia's Kamchatka and Chukotka. It supplies around 40% of the US seafood catch.
geography: Bounded by the Aleutian Islands to the south and the Bering Strait, just 82 km wide, to the north.
water: Sea ice forms in winter and melts in spring, fuelling huge plankton blooms.
life: Walruses, Steller sea lions, northern fur seals, gray and bowhead whales, king and snow crabs, pollock and salmon.
human: The Alaska pollock fishery, among the world's largest; Indigenous Yup'ik and Iñupiat communities.
threats: Loss of sea ice; the snow crab population crashed after a 2018–2019 heatwave, closing the fishery in 2022–23.
seafloor: A wide continental shelf in the northeast and the deep Aleutian Basin (about 4,000 m) in the southwest. In the Ice Age the shelf was dry land, Beringia, across which people reached the Americas.
climate_weather: Seasonal sea ice drives the ecosystem; the 2018–19 ice-free winters and heatwave triggered the collapse of the snow crab fishery.
ecosystems: Walrus, Steller sea lions, northern fur seals, seabirds in millions, and the pollock and king crab fisheries.
history: Vitus Bering's expeditions (1728, 1741); Russian America and the 1867 Alaska purchase.

name: Weddell Sea
summary: A major source of Antarctic Bottom Water and the resting place of Shackleton's Endurance.
overview: A large sea of the Southern Ocean east of the Antarctic Peninsula, partly covered by the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf. It produces much of the cold, dense Antarctic Bottom Water that spreads through the world's ocean.
geography: Between the Antarctic Peninsula and Coats Land.
water: Among the clearest seawater ever measured; brine from freezing sea ice sinks to form bottom water.
life: Emperor penguins, Weddell seals, crabeater seals, krill and the world's largest known fish breeding colony (about 60 million icefish nests found in 2021).
human: Scientific stations; proposed as a marine protected area.
threats: Warming and sea-ice change; krill fishing.
seafloor: Deep shelf and abyssal plain; the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf covers its southern part.
climate_weather: The main source of Antarctic Bottom Water. Its clockwise gyre traps thick sea ice.
ecosystems: Emperor penguin colonies, Weddell seals and, in 2021, a vast colony of ~60 million nesting icefish found on the seabed.
history: Shackleton's Endurance was crushed by ice here in 1915; its wreck was found in 2022 at about 3,008 m.

name: Ross Sea
summary: Often called the most pristine marine ecosystem left, and protected by a large MPA since 2017.
overview: A deep bay of the Southern Ocean, often called the last largely intact marine ecosystem on Earth. It hosts the world's largest marine protected area (1.55 million km², established 2017).
geography: Bounded by the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest ice shelf in Antarctica, and Victoria Land.
water: Very cold, nutrient-rich water and huge polynyas (open-water areas within the ice).
life: Antarctic toothfish, Adélie and emperor penguins, Weddell seals, orcas and minke whales.
human: Science and limited toothfish fishing outside the protected area.
threats: Toothfish fishing pressure, warming.
seafloor: Contains the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest floating ice shelf (about the size of France).
climate_weather: Polynyas produce sea ice and dense water; considered one of the least altered ocean ecosystems.
ecosystems: Antarctic toothfish, Adélie and emperor penguins, Ross Sea orcas and Weddell seals.
history: Ross discovered it in 1841. The Ross Sea MPA (2016) was the first large high-seas MPA, about 1.55 million km².

name: Persian Gulf
summary: A hot, hyper-saline shallow sea whose corals survive extremes that kill corals elsewhere.
overview: A shallow, very warm and salty sea of about 251,000 km² between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, holding some of the world's largest oil and gas reserves.
geography: Bordered by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar and the UAE; connected to the Gulf of Oman through the Strait of Hormuz.
water: Summer surface temperatures exceed 34 °C, some of the hottest seawater on Earth, and salinity tops 40 PSU.
life: Its corals survive extreme heat; it supports dugongs (one of the largest populations outside Australia), green turtles and pearl oysters.
human: Oil, gas and around a fifth of the world's oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz; desalination plants supply drinking water.
threats: Brine discharge, heat-driven coral bleaching, coastal reclamation and oil pollution.
seafloor: Shallow (average ~35 m), formed as a foreland basin of the Zagros mountains; dry land during the last ice age.
climate_weather: Some of the hottest seawater on Earth (over 35°C in summer) and very salty; its corals tolerate heat that would kill others.
ecosystems: Corals, dugongs, seagrass and pearl oysters.
history: A pearling centre for millennia; the 1991 Gulf War spill was one of the largest oil spills ever.

name: Tasman Sea
summary: Between Australia and New Zealand, a marine-heatwave hotspot.
overview: The sea between Australia and New Zealand, about 2,300 km wide, famous for rough seas and the warm East Australian Current.
geography: Bounded by southeastern Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand, with Lord Howe Island in its north.
water: The East Australian Current is strengthening and warming, making this one of the fastest-warming ocean regions.
life: Southern right whales, fur seals, great white sharks, albatrosses and kelp forests.
human: Fishing and shipping between Australia and New Zealand.
threats: Marine heatwaves and loss of giant kelp.
seafloor: Reaches about 5,943 m; the sea opened 85–52 million years ago as Zealandia separated from Australia.
climate_weather: The East Australian Current is warming it rapidly, making it a marine heatwave hotspot.
ecosystems: Lord Howe Island's southernmost coral reef and Tasmanian giant kelp forests (over 95% lost since the 1940s).
history: Named after Abel Tasman (1642).

name: Hudson Bay
summary: A huge inland sea where polar bears depend on seasonal ice.
overview: A vast inland sea of about 1.23 million km² in northern Canada, frozen for much of the year.
geography: Bordered by Nunavut, Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec; connected to the Atlantic through Hudson Strait.
water: Low salinity from many rivers; ice-free only from about July to October.
life: Polar bears that hunt seals on the sea ice, belugas (tens of thousands gather in the Churchill estuary), walruses and narwhals.
human: Inuit and Cree communities; the port of Churchill.
threats: Earlier ice break-up is shortening polar bears' hunting season and their numbers are falling.
seafloor: Shallow (average about 100 m); the land around it is still rising after the weight of the Ice Age ice sheet was removed.
climate_weather: Ice-covered most of the year; ice-free seasons lengthening, stressing polar bears.
ecosystems: Polar bears around Churchill, beluga whales in summer estuaries, and ringed seals.
history: The Hudson's Bay Company (1670) controlled the fur trade across a vast area.

name: Barents Sea
summary: The Arctic's 'hot spot' of warming, where Atlantic water is pushing north.
overview: An Arctic shelf sea of about 1.4 million km² north of Norway and Russia, kept partly ice-free by Atlantic water.
geography: Bounded by Svalbard, Franz Josef Land and Novaya Zemlya.
water: Warm Atlantic water enters from the southwest; it is warming so fast that scientists describe its 'Atlantification'.
life: The world's largest cod stock (northeast Arctic cod), capelin, herring, walruses, polar bears and red king crab (introduced by the Soviets in the 1960s).
human: Rich fisheries and gas fields.
threats: Rapid sea-ice loss, warming and nuclear waste dumped by the Soviet Union.
seafloor: A broad shelf sea (average ~230 m) warmed by Atlantic water.
climate_weather: Rapid 'Atlantification': sea ice retreating and Atlantic species moving in.
ecosystems: Among the largest cod stocks, capelin, and introduced red king crabs.
history: Willem Barentsz explored it in 1596; it was a WWII Arctic convoy route.

name: Caspian Sea
summary: The largest enclosed inland body of water, salty but not connected to the ocean.
overview: The largest enclosed inland body of water on Earth (about 371,000 km²), technically a lake but salty like a sea. It is shrinking.
geography: Bordered by Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan; fed mainly by the Volga.
water: Salinity about 12 PSU, about a third of the ocean's.
life: About 90% of the world's wild caviar-producing sturgeon (now critically endangered) and the Caspian seal.
human: Oil and gas, fishing.
threats: Falling water levels, which could drop by 9–18 m this century; overfishing of sturgeon; pollution.
seafloor: Shallow north (a few metres) and deep south (about 1,025 m). Its surface lies about 28 m below sea level.
climate_weather: Water level fluctuates with Volga inflow and is now falling due to evaporation and warming.
ecosystems: The Volga delta and coastal wetlands.
history: Ancient trade routes and Baku's oil boom in the 19th century.

name: Andaman Sea
summary: A tropical sea between Myanmar, Thailand and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
overview: A tropical sea of about 600,000 km² in the northeastern Indian Ocean, between Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia and India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
geography: Bounded by the Andaman and Nicobar ridge on the west and the Malay Peninsula on the east; connects to the Strait of Malacca.
seafloor: Reaches about 4,198 m; an active back-arc basin with a spreading ridge and Barren Island, India's only active volcano.
water: Monsoon-driven circulation and large internal waves visible from space.
climate_weather: Hit by the 2004 tsunami; cyclones form in spring and autumn.
life: Reef fish, manta rays, dugongs, leatherback turtles nesting in the Nicobars and saltwater crocodiles.
ecosystems: Coral reefs (Similan and Surin islands, Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park), mangroves and seagrass.
history: The 2004 Sumatra–Andaman earthquake (magnitude 9.1) caused the Indian Ocean tsunami.
human: Tourism (Phuket, Havelock/Swaraj Dweep) and fishing.
threats: Coral bleaching, overfishing and development.

name: Laccadive Sea
summary: The sea bordering southwest India, Sri Lanka and the Maldives, containing the Lakshadweep islands.
overview: A warm sea off southwestern India and the Maldives, also known as the Lakshadweep Sea, rich in coral atolls.
geography: Bounded by Kerala, Sri Lanka, the Lakshadweep islands and the Maldives.
seafloor: Reaches about 4,131 m; the atolls sit on the Chagos–Laccadive Ridge, a volcanic track.
water: Warm water (26–30 °C) with seasonal upwelling off Kerala.
climate_weather: Southwest monsoon arrives here first, usually around 1 June over Kerala.
life: Coral reef fish, tuna, sea turtles, dolphins and the oil sardine that sustains Kerala's fishers.
ecosystems: Atolls, lagoons and seagrass beds.
history: Arab and Indian traders sailed it for centuries; Lakshadweep's people are mostly Muslim seafarers.
human: Fisheries, coconut and growing tourism.
threats: Bleaching in 1998, 2010, 2016 and 2024; sea-level rise for atolls.

name: Gulf of Mannar
summary: A shallow gulf between India and Sri Lanka, home to India's first marine biosphere reserve.
overview: A shallow inlet of the Indian Ocean between southeastern India and Sri Lanka, and one of the richest marine areas in South Asia. Its 21 islands form India's first marine biosphere reserve (1989).
geography: Lies south of Rameswaram and Ram Setu (Adam's Bridge), a chain of shoals linking India and Sri Lanka.
seafloor: Mostly shallow coral and sand; deeper to the south.
water: Warm and clear, with seasonal currents.
climate_weather: Northeast monsoon rains in October–December.
life: Dugongs (one of India's last strongholds), sea turtles, dolphins, over 100 coral species, sea cucumbers and pearl oysters.
ecosystems: Coral reefs fringing the islands, seagrass meadows that feed dugongs, and mangroves.
history: Famous since antiquity for pearl fisheries mentioned by Pliny and Marco Polo.
human: Fishing communities, chank (conch) shell collection and seaweed farming.
threats: Coral mining (now banned), bottom trawling, bleaching and sea-level rise.

name: Sea of Okhotsk
summary: The southernmost sea that freezes regularly, bordering Russia and Hokkaido.
overview: A cold marginal sea of about 1.6 million km² enclosed by Siberia, Kamchatka, the Kuril Islands and Hokkaido. It has the southernmost seasonal sea ice in the Northern Hemisphere.
geography: Bounded by the Russian mainland, Sakhalin, Kamchatka and the Kuril chain.
seafloor: Shelves in the north and the Kuril Basin (about 3,372 m) in the south.
water: Sea ice forms each winter, producing dense water that ventilates the intermediate North Pacific.
climate_weather: Drift ice reaches Hokkaido, the world's lowest-latitude seasonal sea ice.
life: Pollock, salmon, king crab, Steller sea lions, spotted seals, bowhead and right whales.
ecosystems: Sea-ice-edge plankton blooms and drift ice off Hokkaido's Shiretoko (UNESCO).
history: Russian expansion to the Pacific from the 17th century.
human: Pollock, crab and salmon fisheries; Sakhalin oil.
threats: Declining sea ice and oil development.

name: East China Sea
summary: A broad shelf sea fed by the Yangtze, the largest river in Asia.
overview: A marginal sea of about 1.25 million km² between China, Korea, Japan and Taiwan, fed by the Yangtze, Asia's longest river.
geography: Wide continental shelf and the Okinawa Trough, with hydrothermal vents.
seafloor: Wide continental shelf; the Okinawa Trough reaches about 2,716 m and has hydrothermal vents.
water: The warm Kuroshio Current flows along its eastern edge; Yangtze outflow lowers salinity.
climate_weather: Vent fauna in the Okinawa Trough, Nomura's jellyfish blooms, hairtail and yellow croaker.
life: Hairtail, yellow croaker, squid and jellyfish blooms.
ecosystems: Estuarine and shelf ecosystems.
history: Trade routes between China, Korea and Japan; disputes over the Senkaku/Diaoyu islands.
human: Huge fisheries and shipping through Shanghai, the world's busiest container port.
threats: Overfishing, pollution and a summer low-oxygen zone off the Yangtze.

name: Yellow Sea
summary: A shallow sea between China and Korea, named for sediment from the Yellow River.
overview: A shallow sea between China and Korea named for the yellow silt carried by the Yellow River.
geography: Includes the Bohai Sea; bordered by China and the Korean Peninsula.
seafloor: Average depth only about 44 m; it was dry land in the Ice Age.
water: Strong tides and a cold water mass in summer.
climate_weather: Cold, dry winters and monsoon summers.
life: Its tidal flats are a crucial stopover for migratory shorebirds such as the spoon-billed sandpiper and great knot.
ecosystems: Among the largest tidal mudflats on Earth (UNESCO World Heritage, 2019).
history: Coastal trade, Korean War landings at Incheon.
human: Fisheries and land reclamation.
threats: Reclamation destroyed much of the tidal flats; algal blooms.

name: Philippine Sea
summary: A deep marginal sea east of the Philippines, bordered by the Mariana arc.
overview: A vast sea of about 5 million km² east of the Philippines and Taiwan, bounded by island arcs and some of the deepest trenches on Earth.
geography: Bounded by the Philippines, Taiwan, Japan, the Marianas and Palau.
seafloor: On its eastern edge is the Mariana Trench, with the Challenger Deep (~10,935 m), the deepest point on Earth; the Philippine Trench reaches about 10,540 m.
water: Warm surface water; source of the Kuroshio Current.
climate_weather: The most active typhoon nursery on Earth.
life: Tuna, whales, deep-sea snailfish (filmed at 8,336 m in 2022) and coral reefs.
ecosystems: Island reefs and hadal trench communities.
history: The 1944 Battle of the Philippine Sea, one of the largest carrier battles.
human: Fisheries and shipping lanes.
threats: Warming, typhoon intensification.

name: Java Sea
summary: A shallow equatorial sea in the heart of Indonesia.
overview: A shallow, warm sea of about 320,000 km² between Java, Borneo and Sumatra.
geography: Part of the Sunda Shelf, which was dry land during the Ice Age.
seafloor: Average depth about 46 m.
water: Warm, low in salinity due to heavy rain.
climate_weather: Equatorial; heavy rainfall.
life: Coral reefs, sea turtles and important fisheries.
ecosystems: Karimunjawa reefs and mangroves.
history: Battle of the Java Sea (1942); many WWII wrecks, some illegally salvaged.
human: Fishing and shipping; Jakarta is sinking and Indonesia is moving its capital to Nusantara.
threats: Pollution, overfishing and coastal subsidence.

name: Banda Sea
summary: A deep sea in eastern Indonesia, home to the deepest forearc basin on Earth.
overview: A deep sea in eastern Indonesia surrounded by islands and once the source of the world's nutmeg and mace.
geography: Bounded by the Moluccas, Sulawesi, Timor and the Banda Islands.
seafloor: The Weber Deep reaches about 7,200 m, the deepest point of any sea not in a trench system.
water: Part of the Indonesian Throughflow, carrying Pacific water to the Indian Ocean.
climate_weather: Monsoon climate.
life: Hammerhead sharks, blue whales and rich reefs.
ecosystems: Volcanic island reefs.
history: The Banda Islands were the only source of nutmeg; in 1621 the Dutch massacred most of the islanders to control the trade.
human: Fishing and spice farming.
threats: Overfishing, warming.

name: Sulu Sea
summary: A basin sea in the southwest Philippines holding Tubbataha Reef.
overview: A sea between the Philippines and Malaysian Borneo, home to the Tubbataha Reefs, one of the best-protected reefs in Asia.
geography: Bounded by Palawan, Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago.
seafloor: Deep basin surrounded by shallow sills.
water: Warm and isolated from the Pacific's deep water.
climate_weather: Typhoons rarely reach it.
life: Over 600 fish species at Tubbataha, sharks, turtles and manta rays.
ecosystems: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park (UNESCO).
history: The Sultanate of Sulu was a maritime trading power.
human: Fishing and seaweed farming.
threats: Piracy and illegal fishing.

name: Celebes Sea
summary: A deep sea in the Coral Triangle known for mysterious midwater animals.
overview: A deep sea between the southern Philippines and Indonesia's Sulawesi (Celebes).
geography: Bounded by Mindanao, Sulawesi and Borneo.
seafloor: Reaches about 6,200 m; formed as ancient ocean floor about 42 million years ago.
water: Warm surface water; part of the Indonesian Throughflow.
climate_weather: Equatorial.
life: Whale sharks, turtles, tuna and the coelacanth's Indonesian relative (Latimeria menadoensis) found off Sulawesi in 1998.
ecosystems: Coral reefs of the Coral Triangle.
history: Maritime trade routes of the Bajau 'sea nomads'.
human: Fisheries.
threats: Overfishing and blast fishing.

name: Gulf of California
summary: The 'aquarium of the world', a young sea opening as Baja California splits from Mexico.
overview: A narrow sea about 1,100 km long and 160,000 km² in area, separating the Baja California peninsula from mainland Mexico. Jacques Cousteau called it 'the world's aquarium' for its astonishing density of life. It is a young sea, opened over the last 5–6 million years as Baja California has been torn away from the North American mainland.
geography: Bounded by Baja California (west) and the Mexican states of Sonora and Sinaloa (east). The Colorado River once poured into its northern end, but is now almost entirely diverted for irrigation. It contains over 900 islands and islets, including Tiburón, the largest island in Mexico.
seafloor: An active rift: a chain of deep basins (Guaymas, Carmen, Farallón, Pescadero) where the East Pacific Rise spreading ridge links to the San Andreas Fault. Pescadero Basin hosts the deepest known hydrothermal vents in the Pacific (~3,700 m). Guaymas Basin vents bubble through thick sediment and grow oily microbial mats.
water: Strong tides (up to ~7 m in the north) and wind-driven upwelling stir nutrients from the depths, feeding intense plankton blooms. The north is hotter and saltier because of evaporation and little fresh water.
climate_weather: Desert climate on both shores, with very hot summers. Hurricanes from the eastern Pacific sometimes strike, such as Odile (2014). The North American monsoon brings summer storms.
life: Around 900 fish species (about 90 endemic), about a third of the world's marine mammal species including blue, fin, humpback and sperm whales, whale sharks, giant mobula ray aggregations that leap from the water, California sea lions and the endemic totoaba. It is the only home of the vaquita porpoise, the world's rarest marine mammal, with probably fewer than about 10 left (surveys in 2023–2024 sighted 6–13).
ecosystems: Rocky reefs, mangroves, the Cabo Pulmo coral reef, a no-take zone where fish biomass rose by over 400% after protection, and the 244 islands and protected areas listed by UNESCO in 2005.
history: Seri (Comcaac) and other Indigenous peoples fished it for millennia. Spanish explorers mapped it in the 16th century and believed Baja was an island. John Steinbeck and Ed Ricketts' 1940 expedition produced The Log from the Sea of Cortez.
human: Shrimp trawling, sardine and squid fisheries, and growing tourism in Cabo San Lucas and La Paz.
threats: Illegal gillnets set for the totoaba, whose swim bladder is smuggled to China, have driven the vaquita to the edge of extinction. Shrimp bycatch, the lost flow of the Colorado River delta and coastal development are other threats.

name: Gulf of Thailand
summary: A shallow gulf bordered by Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.
overview: A shallow gulf of about 320,000 km² in the South China Sea, bordered by Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.
geography: Between the Malay Peninsula and Indochina.
seafloor: Average depth about 45 m; dry land during the Ice Age.
water: Warm and nutrient-rich.
climate_weather: Monsoon rains; occasional typhoons.
life: Irrawaddy dolphins, dugongs, whale sharks and reef fish.
ecosystems: Mangroves, seagrass and reefs around Ko Tao and Ko Chang.
history: Trade routes of Ayutthaya and Funan.
human: Major fisheries, offshore gas and tourism.
threats: Overfishing, mangrove loss for shrimp farms and bleaching.

name: Adriatic Sea
summary: A long arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkans.
overview: An arm of the Mediterranean between Italy and the Balkans, about 800 km long.
geography: Bounded by Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro and Albania; Venice lies at its head.
seafloor: Shallow in the north (under 100 m) and deeper in the south (about 1,233 m).
water: The Po and other rivers lower salinity in the north; dense northern winter water spills southward.
climate_weather: The cold bora wind and the warm sirocco, which drives Venice's acqua alta floods.
life: Over 1,000 Croatian islands, sea turtles, bottlenose dolphins.
ecosystems: Croatia's 1,200 islands and karst coast.
history: The Venetian Republic dominated it for centuries.
human: Tourism, fishing and ports; Venice's MOSE flood barrier (2020).
threats: Overfishing and nutrient pollution.

name: Aegean Sea
summary: The island-studded sea between Greece and Turkey.
overview: An arm of the Mediterranean between Greece and Turkey, scattered with about 1,400 islands.
geography: Includes the Cyclades, Dodecanese and Sporades; connects to the Black Sea through the Dardanelles.
seafloor: Reaches about 3,544 m; the Hellenic arc volcanoes include Santorini.
water: Clear, warm in summer; Black Sea water flows in at the surface.
climate_weather: Strong summer meltemi winds.
life: Mediterranean monk seals, dolphins and Posidonia meadows.
ecosystems: Island reefs and seagrass.
history: The cradle of Minoan and Greek civilisation; Santorini's eruption around 1600 BCE; the Antikythera mechanism wreck.
human: Tourism, ferries and fishing.
threats: Overfishing, tourism pressure and earthquakes.

name: Tyrrhenian Sea
summary: A deep, volcanic part of the Mediterranean west of Italy.
overview: A deep part of the western Mediterranean bounded by Italy, Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica.
geography: Includes the Bay of Naples and the Aeolian Islands.
seafloor: Reaches about 3,785 m with large underwater volcanoes such as Marsili, Europe's biggest.
water: Gyres and deep water.
climate_weather: Mediterranean.
life: Pelagos Sanctuary for whales in the north.
ecosystems: The Pelagos Sanctuary for whales (shared with the Ligurian Sea).
history: Etruscan and Roman sea routes; Vesuvius buried Pompeii (79 CE).
human: Ports of Naples and Palermo and tourism.
threats: Plastic hotspots (microplastics up to ~1.9 million particles per m² of seafloor).

name: Norwegian Sea
summary: A deep sea where warm Atlantic water cools, sinks and feeds the global overturning circulation.
overview: A deep sea between Norway, Iceland and the Arctic, kept ice-free by the warm Norwegian Atlantic Current.
geography: Bounded by Norway, Iceland, Jan Mayen and the Greenland Sea.
seafloor: Reaches about 3,970 m; the Storegga Slide ~8,150 years ago caused a tsunami that hit Britain.
water: A key part of the Atlantic overturning circulation.
climate_weather: Mild for its latitude thanks to the Gulf Stream.
life: Herring, mackerel, orcas and the world's largest cold-water coral reef (Røst Reef).
ecosystems: Cold-water coral reefs and fjords.
history: Viking voyages.
human: Fisheries, oil and gas, and salmon farming.
threats: Warming and fish-farm pollution.

name: Labrador Sea
summary: A key site where the North Atlantic overturns, forming deep water.
overview: An arm of the North Atlantic between Labrador and Greenland where deep water forms in winter.
geography: Bounded by Canada's Labrador coast and southwest Greenland.
seafloor: Reaches about 4,300 m.
water: Winter cooling makes surface water sink, feeding the deep Atlantic.
climate_weather: Icebergs from Greenland drift south ('Iceberg Alley').
life: Harp seals, cod and seabirds.
ecosystems: Sea-ice and iceberg ecosystems.
history: Vikings sailed past; the Titanic iceberg likely came via here.
human: Fisheries.
threats: Freshening from Greenland melt may weaken deep-water formation.

name: Scotia Sea
summary: A stormy sea between South America and Antarctica, rich in krill.
overview: A stormy sea between South America and Antarctica, at the heart of the Antarctic krill fishery.
geography: Bounded by the Scotia Arc islands, including South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.
seafloor: Reaches about 8,264 m in the South Sandwich Trench.
water: Antarctic Circumpolar Current through Drake Passage.
climate_weather: Some of the roughest seas on Earth.
life: Krill swarms feeding whales, seals and penguins; South Georgia wildlife.
ecosystems: Island ecosystems of South Georgia.
history: Shackleton's open-boat journey to South Georgia (1916).
human: Krill fishing.
threats: Krill fishing pressure, warming.

name: Amundsen Sea
summary: The sea beside the Thwaites 'Doomsday' Glacier, where warm water melts ice from below.
overview: A sea off West Antarctica where the fastest-melting glaciers, Thwaites and Pine Island, meet the ocean.
geography: Off Marie Byrd Land.
seafloor: Deep glacial troughs channel warm water.
water: Warm Circumpolar Deep Water melts ice shelves from below.
climate_weather: Rapid ice-shelf thinning.
life: Emperor penguins and seals.
ecosystems: Polynyas with intense blooms.
history: Named after Roald Amundsen.
human: Research only.
threats: Thwaites, the 'Doomsday Glacier', could add about 65 cm to sea level if it collapsed.

name: Beaufort Sea
summary: An Arctic sea north of Alaska and Canada, home to the Beaufort Gyre.
overview: An Arctic sea north of Alaska and Canada.
geography: Bounded by Alaska's North Slope and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago.
seafloor: Shelf and the deep Canada Basin.
water: The Beaufort Gyre stores Arctic freshwater.
climate_weather: Sea ice most of the year, now melting further each summer.
life: Bowhead whales, belugas, polar bears and ringed seals.
ecosystems: Sea-ice and coastal lagoons.
history: Search for the Northwest Passage.
human: Iñupiat and Inuvialuit communities; oil fields at Prudhoe Bay.
threats: Sea-ice loss and oil development.

name: Greenland Sea
summary: A deep-water formation area between Greenland and Svalbard.
overview: An Arctic sea between Greenland and Svalbard where cold East Greenland water meets Atlantic water.
geography: Between Greenland, Svalbard and Jan Mayen.
seafloor: Reaches about 4,846 m.
water: Deep-water formation feeds the Atlantic overturning circulation.
climate_weather: Sea ice carried south by the East Greenland Current.
life: Narwhals, walruses, hooded seals and polar bears.
ecosystems: Pack ice and polynyas.
history: Whaling grounds from the 17th century.
human: Fisheries.
threats: Warming and sea-ice loss.

name: Irish Sea
summary: A shallow sea between Ireland and Great Britain.
overview: Separated by the North Channel and St George's Channel.
geography: Includes Cardigan Bay and Liverpool Bay; the Isle of Man lies in the middle.
seafloor: Shallow; dumped WWII munitions in Beaufort's Dyke.
water: Mixed by strong tides.
climate_weather: Mild and stormy.
life: Basking sharks, grey seals and harbour porpoises.
ecosystems: Sandbanks and estuaries.
history: Viking raids; Liverpool's port grew from Atlantic trade.
human: Ferries, wind farms and fishing.
threats: Radioactive waste from Sellafield (historically) and overfishing.

name: Gulf of Aden
summary: A young rifting gulf linking the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
overview: A deep gulf between Yemen and Somalia linking the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.
geography: Bounded by Yemen, Djibouti and Somalia.
seafloor: A young spreading ridge reaching about 5,390 m.
water: Monsoon upwelling.
climate_weather: Desert climate with monsoon winds.
life: Sharks, dolphins and reefs.
ecosystems: Coral reefs off Socotra.
history: Ancient incense and spice route; modern piracy hotspot.
human: A shipping lane carrying Suez traffic.
threats: Piracy (peaked 2008–2011) and attacks on shipping since 2023.
